new: The kernel is a program that owns the hardware and mediates everything every other program does. Written in C and loaded by a bootloader, it stays resident in Ring 0. It comes in two main shapes: monolithic (everything in Ring 0, fast, fragile) and microkernel (minimal Ring 0, message-passing, safer and slower), with most real systems sitting somewhere on that spectrum. Its scheduler, anchored mathematically in queueing theory, decides which process gets the CPU next, hundreds of times a second. Linux's CFS, and EEVDF after it, does this in O(log N) using a red-black tree of virtual runtimes. Its virtual memory subsystem maintains a four-level page table per process, accelerated by a translation cache (TLB), and uses page faults productively to implement memory-mapped files and copy-on-write fork. Its filesystem turns a flat array of disk blocks into a tree of inodes and names, made crash-safe by journaling or copy-on-write. Its IPC mechanisms (pipes, signals, shared memory, sockets) are the controlled boundary across which isolated processes can still cooperate. And its security depends entirely on its own correctness, which is why kernel bugs are so dangerous, and why each new mechanism (containers, eBPF) is layered behind further verification.

new: The Morris worm, 2 November 1988: the moment computer security became a discipline. Robert Tappan Morris, a twenty-three-year-old graduate student at Cornell whose father was the chief scientist at the NSA's National Computer Security Center, released a self-replicating program onto the young internet that exploited three vulnerabilities at once: a buffer overflow in the UNIX fingerd service, a debug feature accidentally left on in sendmail, and weak passwords in rsh. Each copy, on landing on a new host, replicated itself to nearby hosts. Morris had tried to avoid re-infecting compromised machines, but one time in seven it copied itself anyway, even onto a machine that said it was already infected, so machines were re-infected dozens of times until they collapsed under the load. Within hours, somewhere between five thousand and ten thousand machines (by rough estimates, about ten percent of the internet of the time) were unusable. Morris was traced within days and became the first person convicted under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986. Within weeks of the worm's release, DARPA funded the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) at Carnegie Mellon, the first organisation tasked with coordinating response to internet security incidents. It became the model for the national CERTs that followed. The internet of 1988 had been built in an era of institutional trust; the Morris worm proved that era over.

new: When your laptop wants to know example.com's IP, it asks its configured resolver: your ISP's, or a public service like Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's 8.8.8.8, usually reached through your home router. If the answer is in the resolver's cache, it comes straight back. If not, the resolver does the actual work, called recursion. It asks one of the root servers for example.com; the root replies, "I don't know, but the com servers do. Here are their IP addresses." The resolver asks one of the com servers; com replies, "I don't know, but the example.com servers do. Here are theirs." The resolver asks one of those; that server is authoritative for example.com and returns the actual IP. The resolver caches the answer for the time to live (TTL) the authoritative server sets (typically 5 minutes to 24 hours) and returns it to the laptop. Total time: usually under 50 milliseconds the first time; until the TTL expires, every later lookup costs one short trip to the resolver, or nothing at all when the laptop's own cache still holds the answer.

new: QUIC (RFC 9000, 2021; the name began as Quick UDP Internet Connections, but the standard treats it as just a name) replaces TCP entirely for HTTP traffic. It runs on top of UDP, the "fire and forget" protocol from Section 01 of Chapter 10, and rebuilds TCP's reliable ordered delivery, flow control and congestion control, and HTTP/2's many streams, with TLS 1.3 encryption built in. The difference: each stream is ordered independently, so a lost packet on stream A no longer holds back stream B. QUIC was developed by Google starting around 2012, rolled out experimentally in Chrome and on Google's servers from 2013, and reached essentially all Chrome users by 2017, years before the IETF standard. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114, 2022) is just HTTP semantics over QUIC. As of 2026 it carries roughly a third of web traffic by volume (nearly all of Google's own, and a large and growing share of Cloudflare's and Meta's) and is climbing toward HTTP/2's share everywhere else.

new: The same-origin policy keeps origin A's code out of origin B. But what if the attacker can inject their own code into origin B's page? Then their code is, by definition, same-origin with B, and can do everything B's legitimate code can do. This is cross-site scripting (XSS), one of the most common web vulnerabilities for two decades running. It comes in three flavours. Reflected XSS: the attacker crafts a URL with malicious script in the part after the ?; the server echoes that part back into the page; the script executes on whoever visits the URL. Stored XSS: the attacker submits malicious script as a comment or profile field; the server stores it in the database; every subsequent visitor's browser executes it. DOM-based XSS: a similar attack carried out entirely in the browser, by page JavaScript that copies part of the URL (after the ? or the #) into the page unsafely.

new: The strongest mitigation in the modern web security stack is Content Security Policy (CSP), first shipped in Firefox 4 in 2011, a web standard since 2016 and supported by every major browser by the late 2010s. CSP is a response header (Content-Security-Policy: …) in which the server declares exactly which origins the browser may load resources from, separately for scripts, styles, images, frames, fonts, fetch destinations and every other resource type. A typical strict policy: script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com; style-src 'self' means: "execute scripts only from the same origin and from cdn.example.com; load styles only from the same origin; reject other sources for those two." (Adding default-src 'none' closes every other kind of resource too.) If an attacker injects a <script src="evil.com/x.js">, the browser sees that evil.com is not in the policy and refuses to load the script. The policy admits no inline code either, so the inline <script> and onerror payloads of Fig 12.9 are refused too: the injection succeeds, the attack does not.

new: In June 1970, in the Communications of the ACM, an IBM researcher named Edgar F. Codd published a paper titled "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks." It was eleven pages long, packed with set-theoretic notation, and proposed something that sounded like a complaint: that the databases of the day were forcing programmers to think about how data was stored when they should only have to think about what data they wanted. The existing approach later came to be called navigational: programmers wrote code that walked pointer to pointer through tree-shaped or network-shaped data structures. He proposed replacing all of that with a single abstraction: the relation, a table of rows in no fixed order (to a mathematician, a set of tuples), queryable by a small algebra of operations that returned more relations.

new: Every public-key system in this chapter (Diffie–Hellman, RSA, and the elliptic-curve schemes ECDH and ECDSA) rests on a problem that is hard for classical computers. In 1994, mathematician Peter Shor, working at Bell Labs, published an algorithm that solves both integer factoring and discrete logarithm in polynomial time on a sufficiently large quantum computer. Shor's algorithm has not been run at cryptographically relevant scales: the quantum computers of 2026 have at most about a hundred error-protected logical qubits (quantum bits), each built from many noisy physical ones, and RSA-2048 would need thousands. When a machine of that size exists, it breaks all current public-key cryptography. The estimated horizon ranges from "within ten years" (optimistic engineering) to "fifty or more" (pessimistic).

new: The two attacks Part III already met end the same way. DNS poisoning (Chapter 11, Section 03; Kaminsky 2008) tricks a recursive resolver into caching a forged answer; combined with no certificate validation, it lets an attacker direct a victim to a server they control. Certificate verification is the defence: even with a poisoned DNS answer, the attacker's server cannot present a valid TLS certificate for the legitimate hostname. BGP hijacking (Chapter 9, Section 06) pulls entire IP prefixes toward whichever autonomous system announces them. In Pakistan/YouTube 2008 the traffic was merely dropped, an outage TLS cannot prevent; a malicious announcer could instead steer it through its own machines. Against that the defence is the same: all your packets may now arrive at the attacker's machines, but those machines cannot complete a TLS handshake for the target's hostname. Every network-layer attack on what you read or send ends in TLS and is neutralised there; only denial of service gets through.

new: The cache as a side channel. In January 2018, Spectre and Meltdown showed that speculative execution (the same machinery that gave us the speed described in Chapter 1, present in essentially every fast CPU since the mid-1990s) could be coerced into reading memory across security boundaries. The trick: a speculative load used the secret to pick which memory location to touch, pulling that location into the cache; even though the CPU threw the speculative work away, the cache kept the location, and an attacker timing reads of the candidate locations could see which one came back fast and so read out the secret byte by byte. The fix needed updates to the processors' own internal code (microcode) and kernel page-table isolation (KPTI, which keeps the kernel's memory unmapped while a program runs, so every system call must switch page tables), and it left a lasting ~5–30% slowdown on syscall-heavy workloads. The cache is not just a performance mechanism; it is also the most expensive side channel in the machine.

new: Every controller in Kubernetes, meaning every piece of logic that maintains some kind of object, is a reconcile loop: a tight loop that observes the current state of the world, compares it to the desired state, and takes whichever action will move current closer to desired. Run forever. The loop is idempotent: if it runs twice without anything changing, the second run does nothing. The loop is robust: if a command fails, the next run observes that the change still hasn't happened and tries again. The loop is stateless: it does not remember what it did last time; it only looks at what is versus what should be. The pattern of declared desired state, observed actual state, continuous reconciliation is borrowed from control theory (Chapter 10's TCP congestion control is the same shape) and runs through the tools that build infrastructure from a written description (infrastructure as code): Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, while Terraform and Pulumi run it only when a person asks, working out the changes needed (the plan) and applying them once.
